utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. I wish everybody a very Happy New Year. Good morning Mr. Gagovic there in Belgrade. So how is the weather in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Cloudy. Cloudy, but warm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. The Hague is covered with snow. This is the heaviest snow I have ever seen in ten years' time. But before we begin today, there are several matters to deal with, so, Mr. Gagovic, would you be kind enough to take off your headphones for the moment. The Chamber will first turn to the Prosecution submissions on the status of exhibits provisionally under seal, which was filed on the 20th of December, 2012. In the decision on the status of exhibits provisionally under seal issued on the 14th of December, 2012, the Chamber instructed the Prosecution to inform it whether the provisional under seal status of exhibits D996 and D997 could be lifted pending the Prosecution's confirmation of the identity of an individual who appears in both exhibits. In the Prosecution submission, the Prosecution informs the Chamber, inter alia, that following its review of D996 and D997, the individual who appears in both exhibits is not a witness for whom protective measures are in place. Therefore, the Chamber is satisfied with the Prosecution's submission and instructs the registry to change the status of both exhibits, i.e., Exhibit D996 and D997 from confidential to public. The Chamber will now turn to the accused's motion for subpoena to Slavko Budimir, filed on the 27th of December, 2012. In the motion, the accused argues that he has made all reasonable efforts to obtain the voluntary co-operation of Slavko Budimir by requesting that he submit to an interview by an investigator and testify as a Defence witness in this case. The accused states that Slavko Budimir has declined this request on two occasions, the most recent occasion being the 21st of November, 2012. However, the Chamber notes that no underlying documents that support the accused's contention have been provided. This time the Chamber will afford the accused the opportunity to file the necessary supporting documentation for this motion by Wednesday, 16th January 2013, COB. In the future, however, in the absence of the necessary supporting material, the Chamber might be constrained not to entertain such requests. Now the Chamber will issue an oral ruling in relation to a MFI exhibit. In the decision on the accused's motion to admit documents previously marked for identification and public redacted version of D1938, issued on the 7th of December, 2012, the Chamber, inter alia, denied admission of MFI Exhibit D2202, an intercept which had been MFI'd and placed under seal on the ground that the accused had failed to make any showing regarding its authenticity. The registry has since informed the Chamber that MFI D2225 is the public redacted version of MFI D2202. Therefore, although MFI D2225 was not included in the accused's motions relating to the 7th of December MFI decision, the Chamber will, in the interests of judicial efficiency, deny admission of MFI D2225 and hereby instructs the Registry to mark it as not admitted. Now, could the Chamber move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then unless there's anything to be raised, we'll hear Mr. Gagovic's evidence. Yes. If the court officer could do this. Yes, good morning, Mr. Gagovic, again. I thank you for your co-operation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Could the witness take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you take a seat and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you be kind again to take off your microphone for a brief moment. Yes. I forgot to raise this. Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Robinson, amongst the statement of Mr. Gagovic, the Chamber has difficulty to see the relevance of paragraphs 6, 7, and 9, so I would like these paragraphs to be redacted. Otherwise, at the end of your examination of the -- Mr. Gagovic, explain the relevance to the Chamber and lead live, if necessary, those paragraphs. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And before the witness puts his headphones back on, I simply wanted to mention that in conformity with previous practice, I believe that a 90(E) advisement to be appropriate here as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you like to make any submission with respect to the issue I raised, i.e., paragraphs, 6, 7, and 9?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, your Excellencies. Good morning, your Excellencies. Good morning to everyone, and Happy New Year. Happy all the holidays. As far as these three paragraphs are concerned, I find it necessary that a responsible commander of the 4th Corps should present the circumstances under which these events took place, because the circumstances dictated the conduct of all the parties. Those were actions, and reactions were chaotic. This witness can confirm this. In the months just before the war, it is relevant to know the deployment of the assets and the personnel of the JNA only in Serb areas. Why only Serb areas? Was it because of the Serbs or because of the JNA that was in jeopardy everywhere? That is very important for the claims in the indictment that concern the closeness between the Serb side in Bosnia and the JNA. The JNA was -- the Serb side was pushed into the war in Bosnia. We were very wary of the JNA as a force because it was a force of the previous regime, a Communist one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, do you have any observation?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. I think the Court has been aware of this general rationale before, and I consider the issue to be the extent to which the particular information was applicable to an argument that had been raised before and which had justified the admission of some material but -- but not other material, and that seemed to be the issue. I'm not sure the accused addressed that directly. I have some -- we'll have some later argument in connection with at least the document in paragraph 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the Chamber is not satisfied with the relevance of these paragraphs, either geographically or substantively, so we'll order these three paragraphs excluded from the statement. Yes. If the court officer -- court deputy could help the witness to have the earphones on. Yes, Mr. Gagovic. Thank you again. Before you start giving evidence --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- I would like to draw your attention to a particular Rule here at the Tribunal. Under this Rule, Rule 90(E), you may object to answering a question from the Prosecution or the accused or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer will incriminate you. When I say "incriminate," I mean that something you say may amount to an admission of your guilt for a criminal offence or could provide evidence that you have committed an offence. However, even if you think your answer will incriminate you and you do not wish to answer the question, the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question, but in such a case, the Tribunal will make sure that your testimony compelled in such a way shall not be used as evidence in other case against you for any offence other than false testimony. Mr. Gagovic, do you understand what I have just told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. I understood everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Gagovic.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you given a statement to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read that statement and signed it?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have read and signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have the B/C/S version before you?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is everything in the statement an accurate reflection of what you said?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to ask you these same questions today, would your answers be generally the same?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: I believe they would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I tender this statement, 1D1 -- 1D6180.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, with the redaction I referred to. That's 92 ter statement will be admitted into evidence. Shall we give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit D2738. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, turning to the associated exhibits, we would ask permission for the Court to add three of those documents to our 65 ter list. Those are numbers 1D10065, 67, and 68.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Have they been uploaded into e-court?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: As far as I know, but I can check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the court officer could confirm. By way of example, can we see the 1D10065? Are we having a difficulty problem with the videolink?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Robinson, I take it that you are not tendering 1D6184, which has been referred to in para-9.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. In light of the decision of the Chamber, we won't tender that. Looking through e-court quickly, it looks like the three documents that I mentioned are in e-court but not with translations, so if that's the case, we'll either have to lead them live or give up on those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. You have no objection, Mr. Tieger, as to 1D1836 and 1D4202?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Actually, Mr. President, first of all, 1D01836 is already in evidence as P01509.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. P1509. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. With respect to 1D04202, I looked at that in connection with the previous standards that I understood to have been established for admission in this Chamber, a matter that I've discussed on other occasions with Mr. Robinson, and I tried to reconcile it with some of the recent rulings concerning documents that reflected the statements by SDS officials promulgated through official organs clearly intended to reach the public and to state their position on various matters during the course of the war. This document seemed, as far as I can tell, is a reflection of information provided by a particular source. This witness can tell us nothing about who that source is or the relative accuracy of this information. It's -- my view was that if the other documents I mentioned didn't come in in light of what I would consider to be their probative and reliable nature on their face, this -- this kind of document would -- would fall somewhere below it in terms of admissibility. As the Court is aware and as Mr. Robinson is aware, I'm generally an advocate of broad admission and the assessment of the totality of the evidence, but in this case I'm trying to reconcile the standards in this courtroom and the various documents which are tendered, and for that reason I bring the Court's attention to the nature of this document and the comments, the limited comments, made by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, would you like to respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think with respect to that document, what the witness said to it -- said about it in paragraph 5 is that he can agree that the contents of the reports we received from the corps chief of security looked exactly like this. So I think it would probably be more useful to have that document put to him and see what he could say about the document before you decide about its admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. The Judges cannot see the e-court documents at the moment, but with that understanding, shall we continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In addition, there seems to be some further problem, but let's give it a try and continue, see how it evolves. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Dr. Karadzic is having trouble actually finding things on -- getting e-court also, but --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Your Honours, good morning. I'm unable to hear the English channel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] -- in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yeah, that's the problem that I referred to.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] The witness is able to hear the B/C/S, but I'm unable to listen to the English channel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we rise for ten minutes and try to sort it out in the meantime. The Chamber will rise for ten minutes. --- Break taken at 9.34 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gagovic, you are hearing me in your language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am. I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then let's continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to read Colonel Gagovic's summary in the English language, and then I will shed light on the document 4202. [In English] Milosav Gagovic was a professional soldier. In 1992, when war broke out in Bosnia and Herzegovina, he was the assistant commander for logistics of the 4th Corps of the JNA in Sarajevo. From May 1992, he was acting commander of the 4th Corps of the JNA. Milosav Gagovic considers that the replacement of the single-party social system with multi-party brought turmoil to the ethnic and religious relationships between the people in BH. The political disagreements between the SDA, SDS, and HDZ transferred to their people. Alija Izetbegovic stressed his wish to create an Islamic state, whereas Radovan Karadzic stressed that everyone in BH should receive equal treatment. During the fighting, Colonel Milosav Gagovic noted that all the power in the authorities in B and H was concentrated on Alija Izetbegovic, who was able to influence many events in B and H. To realise their goals, the SDA and the HDZ began to illegally form paramilitary and police forces. Milosav Gagovic was also aware that a known terrorist trained members of the HDZ paramilitary units. Further, the Croatian authorities released prisoners who had been convicted for the most serious crimes of extremes -- extremism, terrorism, and radicalism.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. Karadzic, was that not the part of what has been excluded? Yes. Was that the point, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, and I believe other portions of the anticipated summary also contain some of the redacted material. So the accused should be attentive to that, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you follow, Mr. Karadzic? Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Okay. Then I will skip the next paragraph concerning JNA, Listica, Mostar. I do hope it's going to be relevant. Milosav Gagovic considers that Alija Izetbegovic used the referendum regarding the independence of BH to brand the Serbs as an enemy of the other two peoples. This then began a witch hunt against Serbs in Sarajevo which began with the killing of a Serbian wedding guest. Further attacks took place and armed gangs stormed apartments at night, looting them and abusing the people inside. Members of the paramilitary groups were seen parading in villages and singing chauvinistic songs, insulting Serbs. Serb civilians formed guards at the entrances to buildings and barricades were elected. Families began receiving threats over the phone, and abusive notes were thrown into letterboxes. At the time, many people left their properties. Further, HDZ paramilitary formations murdered over 30 Serbian elderly, women, and children in Gornji Malovan village on the 5th of April, 1992. The first armed attack against the JNA followed shortly after this. On the 22nd of April, 1992, Muslim forces attacked the civilian population of Ilidza. A number of JNA soldiers were attacked on the way to assist the civilians. Between 22nd of April and the 2nd of May, 1992, Muslim paramilitary groups attacked the military district group and barracks almost every night. These then became general attack against the JNA features in Sarajevo. The paramilitary -- the military hospital in Sarajevo and the Marsal Tito Barracks were under blockade, and the airport in Butmir was attacked too. JNA forces captured Alija Izetbegovic when he landed in Sarajevo, as they believed he was in charge of the army that carried out the attacks against the JNA. Negotiations were held, and the attacks on the JNA were suspended on 2nd and 3rd of May. However, despite agreements previously made, a convoy was attacked and JNA soldiers were killed. A few soldiers were captured and imprisoned on which occasions they were beaten abused. Further attacks were launched on the JNA military features every day and the soldiers were under blockade at the barracks. Throughout this the JNA command attempted to resolve the matters peacefully by reaching agreements. Muslim paramilitary units attacked JNA depots to obtain large quantities of weapons. Many weapons had already been removed by them illegally. Although agreements had been made to allow the JNA to remove some weapons from the depots, Muslim forces attacked the vehicles carrying these weapons and removed them from the lorries. Milosav Gagovic was aware that Muslim forces used civilian features to attack the Serb positions. Muslim forces constantly opened fire against the Serbian residential areas and the JNA barracks. If the Serbian artillery attacked parts of the city, these were attacks against noticed military targets. Milosav Gagovic, colonel, was co-operated with the legal representatives of -- and ministers in the corps' zone of responsibility. He did not co-operate with any paramilitaries. Crisis Staffs in those areas formed Territorial Defence units where Serbs were the majority. The JNA and Serbian Territorial Defence were not working towards the division of Sarajevo. Their only task was to protect their homes and their families. And that would be the short summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, sir, I'd like to ask you to look at a document which we have assigned the number 1D04202. I hope you have it.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's not the document we have in e-court now. Can we please have 1D04202. Yes, this is it. Colonel, sir, please look at the date, the heading and the addressee, and then please turn to page 2, the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see the paragraph which reads: "The nature of these meetings is still at the level of initial organising efforts," et cetera, and then the sentence: "He claims that he toured the areas of Sandzak, his native, Prijepolje, Rudo, Foca ..." and then you can turn the page.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "... Visegrad and other areas in the Drina valley." And now he says here that the best organised illegal units are Muslim units in Foca, that they have 2.000 members, that's units for special operations are being formed and they should be given priority, that all the vital facilities in Bosnia-Herzegovina are being monitored and that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic. Mr. Karadzic, it's very leading. Mr. Karadzic -- Mr. Tieger, would you like to say anything? I remember you rose.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. No, the -- you anticipated me, and I think that's particularly the case in the context of the objection that was raised and the ostensible purpose for bringing this document to the witness's attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, would you like to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I actually asked Dr. Karadzic to ask the witness a general question about this document before calling his attention to the specific part of the text and I think he should do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, were you able to have a look at page 3?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you familiar with these issues? Did you learn them from this document or did you know of these issues from your general knowledge, and how does this fit into your knowledge of the events ahead of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: I did say in my statement that we at the corps command had regular briefings by the corps commander -- or with the corps commander of the situation in the area of responsibility of the 4th Corps. Therefore, all the developments taking place in that period were the subject of our briefings, including this particular information. The undersigned Colonel Simovic briefed us on this matter and told us that the eastern part of Bosnia was more busily working with the Sandzak area and the area in Montenegro. So that when I saw this document, I clearly said that I was aware of these issues. Not only concerning these areas but also other areas that were matter of our briefings. Though I don't think that the name of our former chief of the 4th Corps, Fikret Selimovic, who was by that time already on the side of those who were forming the SDA paramilitary formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I was waiting for interpretation. Can you look at the first paragraph on page 3, which reads that some -- that he wanted to attack some military depot but that the SDA leadership would not give their consent. Can you tell us what -- can you tell us what was the influence of the SDS over the JNA at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, the SDS didn't have any influence over the JNA at the time, and this was true of all the other political parties. At the time, the JNA was still the people's army, the army of all the various ethnicities, and was recruited from the ranks of all the various ethnicities except for those who refused to respond to call-ups, and at that time it was already something that members of the Muslim and Croat ethnicity did, and we already had the Rump Presidency at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As for your command, in early December of 1991, were there still senior officers of Muslim and Croat ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. General Ante Karanovic, the chief of staff, was Croat. There was Rasim Delic who was the operative in the operations department. There was Muharem Nadza, colonel, and there were quite a few junior officers, there were lieutenant-colonels who were in the command corps -- in the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And who was the commander of the 10th Brigade at Lukavica?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: It was Kari Kasanovic [phoen], Lieutenant colonel, and the head of the artillery regiment --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness be asked to slow down and repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gagovic, could you -- could you repeat your answer, and when answering the question, please slow down for the benefit of the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. [Interpretation] I said that the corps command at the time included Muslim and Croat senior officers. The chief of the staff was General Ante Karanusic [phoen], a Croat, a native of Split. The operations officer in the first sector was Rasim Delic who later became the commander of the armed forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina; that's to say the federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. There was Colonel Nadjak, a Muslim, the chief of ON Nov sector. The chief of the Motorised Brigade, Enver Kari Kasanovic. He was a lieutenant-colonel of the JNA. The commander of the 4th Mixed Artillery Regiment at Kiseljak, Lieutenant-Colonel Polutak. The commander of the 6th Proletarian Brigade in Doboj was Lieutenant-Colonel Cazim Hodzic. They were officers who held key positions and they were Croats and Muslims. Of course, there were more officers also among those who held lower-level positions across the brigades until 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: One more question, Colonel. On page 3, it is stated that he asked that a unit of specialists be set up for covert execution or assassination. Was there anything that hinted at this?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we knew of a list of people who were members of the JNA of Serb and Montenegrin ethnicities who were on this list for assassination or liquidation. There were already telephone threats to family members of these JNA officers, threatening messages placed in their letterboxes. The flats of some of the officers were stormed as well. We knew that they planned their quiet liquidation, because we knew that they would offer a taxi service to transport senior officers from the point of Assembly to unknown locations where they would be subjected to blackmails or liquidations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I have no further questions based on this document. I would now like to tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have to under the circumstances I'm afraid I have to renew the same objection. I cannot see how the fact that this witness received the document somehow cleanses it of its underlying issues of unreliability. To analogise to the case I raised before, in comparing it to documents that had been rejected, it would be as if someone said, "I received the official SDS organ which contained the interview of this SDS official who wanted us to hear these things." Now, presumably that wouldn't have changed the Court's ruling in that case, although, as the Court is aware, I continue to believe that such information shouldn't be admitted. In this case, however, we have an informant, about whom we know nothing, about whom the witness apparently knows nothing, and this information which has been the subject of the discussion about whether or not it is sufficiently reliable for admission should -- should be admitted. And nothing the witness said to that added in any way. The witness contextualised it in a sense but that doesn't change the admissibility issue because in the previous case, as I mentioned before, the -- that issue concerning admission, whether it was contextualised, affirmed, or whether it served as impeachment also existed in the previous case as impeachment, so we get to the underlying issue of -- apparently of reliability, and that's -- which is why the accused was asked to address this document. And we now understand that this witness has been receiving information of this sort, which is essentially a statement from the agent Semso about whom we know nothing, which is much less than we knew about the person who was making the statement that we -- that was tendered in the instance I described before but was rejected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The simple answer to this is this goes entirely to weight, and you've admitted before many documents similar to this on behalf of the Prosecution reports of state security, reports of Muslim police organs who took information from other people, so I don't think that this is inadmissible for the reasons stated by Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, the Chamber agrees with Mr. Robinson's objection. The witness confirmed some part of the document, and as you indicated, contextualised the document. We'll admit it as Exhibit D2739. But there seems again to be another problem with the videolink. Just let us check.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the meantime, may I ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Tieger. Yes. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, just to raise one point and not to -- this is not to revisit the ruling itself, just to make a point because these issues are recurring and sometimes it's useful at the moment to make an observation that may bear on future tendering and discussions of admission. First of all, I would ask the Court in the future to consider the circularity of the confirmation. I mean, you say that the witness confirmed the information. The witness was getting this information. That was the source of his information. So there's a circular aspect to this. He's saying I knew about this based on this kind of document. Again, that has the problem. Secondly, I think it will bear on and I will -- we -- I think it sheds light on admission and tendering of -- of other types of documents, the type I described, and that's all I wanted to mention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's deal with the issue when it arises. Mr. Karadzic, have you completed your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, your Excellency. In -- on page 18, in line 25 and on page 19, line 1, Mr. Tieger mentioned the SDS out of the context. I don't see what this sentence means at all. This isn't a report by the SDS but by an official organ of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson knows what the reference meant and can explain it to the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's leave it there. Mr. Karadzic, the witness statement said that he was an acting commander of the JNA 4th Corps in Sarajevo in June 1992. Could you ask him what military positions he took after that and when he retired.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, who was the commander of the 4th Corps before you took up that position?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: It was General Djurdjevac, Vojislav Djurdjevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before the next commander was appointed, you were acting commander, were you not?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Acting commander of the 4th Corps. Stand-in commander of the 4th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So acting commander would be different from the stand-in commander, would it not?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in that position for?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: From the 11th of May until the 20th of May when the 4th Corps of the JNA was reformed or transformed. And I stayed in Lukavica until the 1st of June because of the units that were under a blockade in the barracks in Sarajevo. I stayed until the blockades were lifted, and the last was -- blockade was lifted on the 5th of June at the Lukavica barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall when it was that General Mladic came to the 2nd Military District and who had appointed him?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: General Mladic came to the 2nd Military District on the 10th of May. He took up the position of acting commander of the military district, and he was appointed by the national secretary for People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall was the decision taken significantly ahead of the outbreak of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if it was taken earlier on, but it was Milutin Kukanjac who held that position before him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What became of you later? What were the positions that you held subsequently and until what time?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: After this position, I applied for retirement, but before that I used up my annual leave for three months, and officially it was on the 1st of November, 1992, that I was retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, I don't have any further questions for you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gagovic, as you have noted, your evidence in chief has been admitted in most part in written form, i.e., through your written statement. Now you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel. I presume you can hear me. It seems --

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning. I can hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excellent. Colonel, I want to ask you about a number of documents, in particular intercepted telephone conversations in which you participated. I noted in your Dragomir Milosevic testimony that at one point you asked one of the attorneys why they -- why that person hadn't shown you a particular intercept that you considered existed reflecting a conversation you had, and I'll try to put as many of the precisely relevant ones to you as I can at the moment. First, Colonel, I would like to ask you about 65 ter 30743. And for the benefit of the registrar who will be showing you documents and who may already be aware of the organisation of the binder of hard copies, they are presented in D order, P order, and then 65 ter order, all of which are presented numerically. So the 65 ters will be found toward the back of the binder, and this one is 30743. Now, Colonel, I can play you a portion of this if necessary, but as I said, I understood from your Dragomir Milosevic testimony that you were aware of the fact that many telephone conversations had been intercepted and recorded, and so in the interest of expediency, I'm presenting you with the transcript of those conversations. And this is one that is dated the 11th of May, 1992. And if you look --

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And it's between -- first, as we see in the transcript, between yourself and General Mladic. And you are advising him that Baros is on the phone. And then General Mladic goes on to speak with Mr. Baros, and I'll ask you about that in a minute. At this time -- at this time, Colonel, 11 May, where -- where were you and General Mladic located?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: I was in Lukavica --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: -- at the barracks called Cedo. General Mladic came to Lukavica from time to time. He came on the 10th to tell us that he had assumed the duties of the commander of the 2nd Military District, and he was moving from unit to unit getting to know people, and he met General Baros by telephone. Because Baros did not have his own telephone he was using mine, and contact was made with him from one radio to another because he was in the Marsal Tito Barracks. You have this conversation, which I didn't know about, because out of decency and subordination I did not listen to everything, but I know that Baros was told that Mladic had taken up the place of General Kukanjac as commander of 2nd Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. Now, as we see from the discussion as it continues, Baros raises the issue of people coming to the gates, and in that case that would have been, as you've explained, to the Marsal Tito Barracks; is that right, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Concerning these people that Baros is talking about, they were practically civilians who were intimidated in the city of Sarajevo. They were leaving their homes and fleeing to the Marsal Tito Barracks, which was the closest one to them, being located in the centre of the city, near the railway station.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Colonel, you've indicated that out of decency and subordination you didn't listen to the entire conversation, but as we continue in the discussion, and I turn your attention to the fourth page of the transcript, the B/C/S transcript before you, we see that General Mladic advises Baros that Gagovic is listening, and he will continue, and then you and Baros can continue the conversation that had begun before you got General Mladic on the line.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But before that, the general warned me that I can continue with Baros.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. I can see that in the transcript. And after returning now to the earlier part of the discussion shortly after General Mladic began talking with Baros and Baros identified the nature of his concern about people at the Marsal Tito Barracks, General Mladic reassures him and tells him to hold on tight and that negotiations will proceed that day concerning release of property, people, and weapons; correct? And I think you'll find that on the second page of your transcript.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, Baros was preoccupied with the civilian population that was at the Marsal Tito Barracks. There were many families, including women and children; families, many of them of military personnel; and some families whose men had already left Sarajevo, leaving them behind. And there was pressure from Muslim military units to surrender, leave behind all the weapons. Baros said there was no danger that they would do that, because he was prepared to defend the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, and General Mladic offers him further reassurance about holding tight, and that is when he reminds him that you are still in a better position than they, meaning the Muslims are, that they have been sealed off. "The entire town has been sealed off, and the entire Muslim population. They can't touch you. I will put it to them today in no uncertain terms, because if they dare touch a single hair on the head of any of our members or on the head of any member of our soldiers' families --"

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, I don't know how much you know about the environment of Sarajevo. Many areas in Sarajevo and around were populated by Serbs, and in those areas Serbs self-organised themselves to defend their homes and property. That is the kind of encirclement surrounding that Mladic was talking about. And there were daily raids by Muslim units on all sides that created panic among the Serb population, intimidating them so that they would leave even those peripheral areas like they left the central areas of Sarajevo. You know, I had my own private apartment. I wanted to live in Sarajevo among my friends, but I had to relocate my family because there were daily threats. Those were the paramilitary units that were supported and given incentives by the authorities. They wouldn't have been doing those things if they had no support from the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel. Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: And when I say authorities, I mean the authorities led by the president of the Presidency, Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, I have a limited amount of time with you. I -- this is -- these are matters that you had an opportunity to and in fact did raise in the statement you provided the Defence. I'm asking you specific questions about certain issues that arise, and in this particular case about this intercept. I will appreciate it in future questions if you can concentrate on the issue at hand, the question raised, and you can leave it to the Defence if they want to ask you for further elaboration of the context or reasons for those issues. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just before the break, Mr. President, I would tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit P6069. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gagovic, we'll have a break for half an hour and resume at 3 past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any problem with the videolink?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if that's directed toward -- okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gagovic, do you hear me in your language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Now we can see you, Mr. Gagovic. Please continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, I'd next like to turn to another conversation that took place on the 19th of May. This time first between you and Lieutenant-Colonel Jankovic and then Jankovic and General Mladic, and that's found at -- that's 65 ter 30775. I'll give you just a moment to orient yourself on that transcript, Colonel. It's not terribly long, and as you should see from a glance, it is another occasion on which you answered a --

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- answered a phone call and put General Mladic on the line. And again, this is about the -- initially about the evacuation of the barracks issue, as you can see; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General Mladic explains to -- seeks information from Jankovic about what the Muslim interlocutor wants, and learns, as you see in the first page of the transcript, weapons in the same state they found them in, and General Mladic talks about the circumstances in which they, and particularly the Muslims, will be able to enter the barracks, that is, when they pass the separation line Jankovic indicates they want it before and General Mladic says that won't happen. I take it that's consistent with your recollection of circumstances at the time.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: This was a relocation of the recruits from the Marsal Tito Barracks after the lifting of the blockade. Jankovic was there with his team to get things done, to relocate the barracks. However, there was a dispute because the representatives of the Muslim side insisted that nothing can be removed from the barracks apart from the personal belongings of the recruits and officers. However, there were many teaching aids in the barracks, although it may sound strange to you that we considered artillery and other pieces as teaching aids. So Mladic was not was not agreeable to that manner of evacuation. Instead, he wanted a real assessment made as to what can be removed and what cannot, and the objective was to relocate the recruits somewhere in the area of Grbavica. I just established this connection, did not participate in this conversation, but you know that all the telephone and other communications went through my telephone number, because all the other telephones were cut off apart from mine that was wire-tapped all the time. So nothing could be decided in the corps command without my knowledge or without my intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And -- thank you, Colonel. And again as we saw in the previous conversation which took place on the 11th, General Mladic reassures Jankovic in this case in two ways. Number one -- and you can find this on page 2 of your transcript. Number one, he explains that -- that Jankovic is in a better position than the Muslims, and he says, "We can stay in our barracks a year. It's not the barracks which lack food in Sarajevo." And then he also explains that if there is a threat coming from the Muslim side that there will be dire consequences. That's the section you'll see related to bringing in cisterns, that is Sarajevo. Then he should bring cisterns in as happened in Mostar. "Tell Jovo Divjak that him and I know one another very well." And then he continues, "But he can bring in a cistern, but in that case he would sentence first himself and then entire Sarajevo to death." So in both conversations, Colonel, is it correct that General Mladic was offering reassurance to the other military officials he was speaking to by saying their situation was better than the Muslims' and that the Muslims should not dare to take action because there would be extreme consequences if they do; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to go into that conversation between Mladic and Major or Lieutenant-Colonel Jankovic, simply because I did not follow that conversation after making contact. And I made the contact because, as I told you before, my telephone was the only one available to make contact with the corps command. Mladic, like all the negotiators, wanted to take as much as he could, and there were threats to officers and personnel in the Marsal Tito Barracks. This reference to cisterns filled with explosives that would be driven up to the barracks was one of these threats, and such a cistern would have the effect of an atomic bomb. But Mladic was telling Jankovic that these were empty threats, a shot in the dark, as it were. That's how I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Turning -- turning to the authenticity or foundation for the admissibility of intercepted conversations, I'm wondering if the Prosecution can advise us if this particular intercept is among those in the record of the case which was identified by the intercept operators or their supervisors as being an authentic intercept. And the reason I raise that is because of the fact that we've been trying to have our intercepts admitted, and the Prosecution made a filing in December basically saying that essentially we'll have to call the Muslim or Croat intercept operators back if we want to have our intercepts admitted. So if that's going to be the way we have to proceed, then I want to make sure that before the Prosecution has any intercepts admitted that there's some foundation in the record that it's been identified by the intercept operators or witnesses as one of those which was authentic and reliable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You did not object to the admission of previous intercepts, because the witness was one of the interlocutors.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But here Mr. Gagovic does not appear.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: He does, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Other than answering the phone and passing it to Jankovic, but he doesn't appear in the substance of the conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger, would you like to respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I would. Thank you. First of all, I can -- let me respond directly to Mr. Robinson by saying that this -- this was authenticated in P4635, row 453, but more to the point, I think -- I think it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. If it has been authenticated in that exhibit, Mr. Robinson would withdraw his objection, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. This will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah. But we're not trying to -- we are not and were never trying to raise unnecessary hurdles to the admission of intercepts. I think our acknowledgement in the filing we made was consistent with the position we've taken about the intercepted conversations and their reliability overall. So I don't -- I don't want to sign on to the representations made by Mr. Robinson. And finally, there maybe intercepts which -- that I'll be tendering here which are not necessarily authenticated. So I -- sorry, I know you don't want academic discussions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- but we'll get there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. This will be admitted as Exhibit P6070.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, in paragraph 39 of your statement, you made some observations about bombings or bombardments in Sarajevo. I wanted to -- to draw your attention to one contemporaneous event about which you were aware involving the bombardment of Muslim settlements in the area about which you were contacted by a man named Zekerijah Smajic. I take it you recall Mr. Smajic who was a well-known journalist from Jutel?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And just so the Court is aware, Jutel was a media outlet which was somewhat of a symbol of multicultural Yugoslavia. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gagovic, could you kindly repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was Jutel's intention. It was set up as a Yugoslav broadcasting channel, but it did not contribute much to the progress of the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina. On the contrary, sometimes even fuelled up the ongoing conflict between the peoples in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we turn to 65 ter 30745, please, and take a look at the discussion that took place between you and Mr. Smajic on the 11th of May, 1992. Now, it's a little bit longer than the other -- the [indiscernible] conversations we looked at, Colonel, so let me try to draw your attention to particular portions and identify where they can be found in your transcript as well as in the English version. So first of all at -- on the first page we see that Mr. Smajic introduces himself, including some mention of his military background, and also identifies himself as an inhabitant of the settlement Bresje. That's found at -- so the introduction I mentioned about the military is found at page 1 of your transcript, and the mention that he's an inhabitant can be found at page 2. He then explains that he got involved in some peace missions after the shocking attack the day before yesterday and visited the settlement of Sokolje. You can see that on page 2 as well. And then as you'll see toward the bottom of page 3 of your transcript, he begins talking about the all-out cannonade including attacks on the settlements Boljakov Potok, Sokolje, and Bresje Brdo of the areas that he had visited yesterday. He continues to tell you that he believes that is in response to or was connected to another shelling aimed at the barracks of Rajlovac but that he says that came from the hill of Zuc and is 99 per cent sure it was a case of intentional provocation. He goes on at -- toward the bottom of page -- excuse me. The -- toward pages 4 and 5 of your transcript, talking about a conversation that he had with Colonel Miletic -- excuse me. You tell him about a conversation you had with Colonel Miletic, and that in response, after hearing Miletic saying that he was being shelled from Brijesko Brdo, you called Abdic and asked for his intervention to stop that in order to prevent the responsive shelling and destroying facilities, houses, and especially prevent killing people. And then Colonel, we also see reference by Smajic to basically again a denial that people from those areas are shelling. That they're all in shelters. Finally two more references I wanted to bring your attention to -- well, first of all, Colonel, and before I go on to the final two references, can I take it given the somewhat dramatic nature of this phone call and the plea we were hearing from Smajic that you recall this conversation and the information you were receiving about the shelling of these three Muslim settlements?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: I remember this conversation well. I knew Mr. Smajic from before. He knew me as well. He knew that the JNA was a mediator for the civilian population, that it protected the civilian population regardless of ethnicity or religious affiliation. That's why he called me. At the same time from Rajlovac, a person called Miletic, who was a director in the military factory, complained of having been shelled, that shells were falling on Rajlovac and the airport which was an auxiliary airport. On the other hand, Hajrija called me to say the same things happened in his area, that mortar shells were falling, that the population was scared, and he asked me to do whatever was in my power to prevent all that. Since Mr. Fikret Abdic represented the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, after the 4th of May in a negotiation with the JNA I talked to Fikret and asked him to talk to Miletic, because I spoke to Miletic as well. I wanted the three of them to find -- find a solution, because it was not just one side that provoked the other. Everybody provoked everybody else. Who was it who started with provocation first is something that I can't answer. And as for Zekerijah's words, that nothing happened in his village, that fire was not opened from his village, it was his village that fire was opened on. There were some renegade Muslim groups that had at their disposal mortars. They would mount those mortars on a lorry, they would fire a projectile or two on a location, then they would change locations, and they never gave a second thought to the place where the projectile would fall. Sometimes there were projectiles fall among their own. Sometimes they fell on the Serbian side. I spoke to all three of them, and at the end, we could not conclude who was it who opened the fire first, where the projectiles came from. Mr. Smajic had been an anti-aircraft officer. He then completed his university studies. He became a journalist. He's still a journalist. He was a good journalist then, and he continued being a good journalist. He's a good man and a good professional. And regardless of his professionalism and knowledge of military issues, I'm sure that he could not devise where the projectiles came from. He could only assume as did I, as did Fikret, and as did Mr. Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Colonel, one the things you told Mr. Smajic was that when he was asking for those salvos and destruction to stop was that the party, and you can look at it in context by which it seems clear you meant the SDS, has significant influence. They are armed en masse. They picked up the arms from Faletici. They have lethal weapons at their disposal. And that's found, Colonel, at page -- the second-to-last page toward the bottom of your transcript. So it's correct, is it not, Colonel, that when Smajic called you to beg for intervention to stop the shelling, you referred to the massive arming of the SDS and their possession of lethal weapons?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that I had an occasion to discuss that. I didn't mention the SDS, because the SDS did not have any weapons as a party. The term that sometimes appears in my conversations and in the conversations conducted by others refers to something that was used by the other side, the Territorial Defence which was a territorial structure among Muslims and Serbs alike is something that they did not want to refer to as the Territorial Defence. They called it the SDS army, because at the same time they called their own armed forces the Territorial Defence. However, the SDS as a party, as far as I know, never had any armed formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel --

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Up to the moment when the Serbian Army was set up, they did not have any army, because members of the Serbian ethnicity responded to the JNA call-ups, and able-bodied men joined units of the JNA, either as former recruits or volunteers. They replaced Muslim and Croat members of the JNA who at that time from the end of 1991 onwards had stopped responding to the JNA call-ups.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that's --

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: You were talking about lethal weapons, something that I mentioned, but I don't believe that I ever used that term, because everybody knows very well what lethal weapons are. At that time, neither side had those. They could only have conventional weapons of the infantry weapons type. I don't know whether I've answered your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender this, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't have any objection, but with respect to this last question and the answer from the witness, I don't think Mr. Tieger was that fair to the witness, because he made his question very general, and then at the end of the question tied it into a particular portion of this transcript. I think it would have been better if he would simply have placed before the witness page -- what appears on the bottom of page 8 of the English, the two answers that relate first to -- with respect to Mr. Krajisnik, and then exactly what Mr. Gagovic is recorded as having said, and ask him the question in light of that, because his attention was never directly called to that particular answer he gave, and I think the answer that he's giving, which seems to be from memory, is not very responsive.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm not sure how accurate that is. I thought I directed the witness's attention to that portion of the transcript explicitly and told him exactly where it could be found in his transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to say anything in front of the witness, but if you look at the answer that the witness gave that's in the transcript, I think if he had read that answer, he would not have given the response that he gave to Mr. Tieger's question. So I don't think it was -- at least the way Mr. Tieger posed the question which started from the general and went to the specific was sufficient to alert the witness to actually read that portion of his answer and make an answer that's responsive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Gagovic, having heard Mr. Robinson and read the remainder of the document, would you like to add anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see here what the Prosecutor alleged, that I connected the arming of the Territorial Defence with the event described to me by Mr. Zekerijah. It seemed that the Territorial Defence had obtained a certain quantity of weapons when it came in conflict with the Muslims in Faletici and that it was stronger and that they had weapons, but those were conventional weapons such as rifles, 79 millimetres and 76.2 semi-automatic weapons. Those were not lethal or destructive weapons, and in that area where that case happened that Zekerijah described, it's not there. It's a different part of the world north-west of Sarajevo in the direction of Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This -- apparently there is no objection to the admission of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me ask the witness the following: I want to draw your attention to have you confirm something you said during the course of your testimony during the Dragomir Milosevic case. And that is in connection with depots and who took ammunition, and you said beginning at page 8690 and extending into page 8691 of the Dragomir Milosevic transcript: "Smaller depots were spread throughout Sarajevo and the environments. The largest one was in Faletici. Paramilitary forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina tried to get into these warehouses to get the weaponry and prior to that they carried out large quantities of weaponry illegally to say so. Then there was conflict between the forces of the Territorial Defence of the Republika Srpska and the BH Federation forces and the majority of the weaponry ended up in the hands of the Army of Republika Srpska." Now, that's a direct quote from the testimony you gave in the Dragomir Milosevic case. Can you confirm that, Mr. -- Colonel Gagovic? I'm not seeking --

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I have not changed that statement with my previous answer. I said the same. Perhaps not in so many words. But in Faletici there was no artillery ammunition. There were no artillery pieces, only the infantry weapons were there, only personal infantry weapons such as rifles, automatic weapons, and machine guns, but not lethal weapons that could be used in the area mentioned by Zekerijah Smajic. It is true that those two armed components conflicted in Faletici and that the territorial forces which belonged to the Serbian side overpowered the other side. They prevailed because they were stronger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, when you referred to the taking of weapons from Faletici in speaking to Mr. Smajic, you're referring to exactly the same event you're talking about in your -- you talked about in your Dragomir Milosevic testimony, that is the taking of weaponry by the members of or people associated with the Bosnian Serb Territorial Defence or, as you say in the Dragomir Milosevic testimony, the Army of Republika Srpska. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: That happened only in the Faletici depot. The two armed components conflicted, the Muslims on the one side, the Serbs on the other side. The Serbs had prevalence and they managed to get hold of the weapons from at that depot. As far as I remember, I testified about that. But I did not mention that in my conversation with Zekerijah. He mentioned something completely different, the arming of the Serbian Army, i.e., the Territorial Defence of Serbia on the one side and the Muslim Territorial Defence on the other. And I still claim that both used to try and get hold of the weapons that belonged to the city of Sarajevo from their weapons -- from their depots, some of them which were in the city of Sarajevo. And when it comes to the operative part and the manoeuvre part of the Territorial Defence, their weapons were stored in Faletici.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, I tender this document. I tender the intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Shall we give the number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit P6071. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In connection with the taking of weaponry by the Bosnian Serbs and their success in Faletici, I want to direct your attention to 65 ter 12028. And this is Mr. Milovan Bjelica speaking in Srpsko Oslobodjenje, a publication set up by the RS on the 27th December 1994. If you turn to -- you'll see the third column of that article, and it begins on the bottom half of the third column. He's asked about how did you arm the people and explains in particular --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Let's make sure that the witness has the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I see from the screen that was just put in front of you, Colonel. If you can direct your attention to the third column, and the question begins, "How did you arm the people ?" And it begins: "Serbian Democratic Party organised all activities related to preparation and organising of people for defence." It talks about taking weapons in various places. And then it concludes at the bottom of that paragraph: "And our greatest success was taking the equipment and weapons from Faletici." And as he continues in the next full paragraph after that, it talks about a confrontation at the -- at Faletici between the forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Bosnian Serb forces and their success in prevailing in that confrontation and pulling out the weapons. Now, I take it that in that respect you can confirm, as you did before, that this is the same event you were talking about, that is the removal of weaponry by Bosnian Serb forces after a confrontation with Muslim forces or BiH forces.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: I have read that part. I believe that this refers to that same event. However, it was not that the weapons were only in Faletici. There was a lot of it in the city of Sarajevo, in many facilities that held the weapons of the Territorial Defence. After that case, the Muslim side made a request to the JNA command, i.e., to the General Staff, to compensate them for the two-thirds of that weaponry, because they believed that that was as much as belonged to them. The General Staff responded favourably and tried to implement that compensation, i.e., to restore the weapons to the Muslim side from the depot in [indiscernible]. Several trucks of weapons arrived and they were supposed to be stored in -- on the premises of the PTT engineering where UNPROFOR soldiers were billeted. General Louis MacKenzie is well aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, can I stop --

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: However, it was agreed that the weapons would not be distributed -- yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm always in the Trial Chamber's hands, but I believe you answered my question and then went on to address some other issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think the Chamber is in agreement with me. Thank you. I tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. This is the same category of documents we dealt with with the Tintor and Mrs. Plavsic statements -- after the fact statements before Christmas recess and I think it falls into the same category. This is a 1994 interview by Mr. Bjelica which is reflecting back on events in 1992, and all the witness has said about it was that it refers to the same event, and so I don't believe that there is any basis for admitting it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have to say these are constantly moving goal posts by the Defence. This -- first of all, the objection raised by the Defence earlier with respect to the Tintor documents that Mr. Robinson has now cited was already a shifting of the standards for admission that existed before, but just dealing with that now, what happened before was that the argument was there was no affirmation of the document. There is affirmation here. In addition, this document can serve as either affirmation or confirmation or corroboration of what the witness said with respect to the Faletici incident, or it would be the basis for potential impeachment of that. I had a discussion with Mr. Robinson some time ago. This is -- the issue about these documents is general reliability. This document is clearly reliable for all kinds of reasons. It's produced through Srpsko Oslobodjenje, a Bosnian Serb -- an RS publication. It's done during the course of the war, not belatedly. Those were all standards Mr. Robinson identified and agreed to in the previous discussions, that is the ones that preceded the Tintor issue. It's affirmed to a significant measure by the witness. There is no reason why the Trial Chamber should be precluded from hearing this evidence. The fact that it doesn't -- if we're going to -- if we're going to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By the way -- just, I'm sorry to cut you off, but my question is this: Not all the documents have been translated and the relevant part was read to the witness and we heard his answer. Do we need to admit this separately in practical terms?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm not sure if that means -- if -- if the issue is -- if -- if what I -- yeah, I think we do, Mr. President. I mean, I paraphrased. I don't mind -- I'm agreeable to the admission of only those portions of the document to which I referred plus any necessary contextualisation introducing the individual, but it cannot be the case, I submit, that we -- we hear the entirety of a document that relates information provided by an unnamed informant about whom we know nothing, but we don't hear precise focused information from an SDS official through an official SDS publication designed for dissemination and to be heard by the public and the world. This is clearly significantly more reliable information and should be admitted for that -- for that reason. Now, I could read -- I could read into the record the entirety of the exchange in the document verbatim, but I did not do so, and this is a faster way of doing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. The Chamber will admit only those part put to the witness. Shall we give the number. 6072. Yes, Exhibit P6072. Please continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Just so I understand, are you admitting that to -- in the context to the witnesses answer as opposed to for the truth for all purposes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That goes to the weight, Mr. Robinson, but I will consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before you do, if I could just be heard on this. This is also something that Mr. Tieger and I are always arguing over and discussing. So let's say that Mr. Bjelica had testified in one of the early -- in the Tadic trial, one of the earlier trials, and had said something like this, and then would you admit his testimony, because if the witness simply said yes that talked about the same event, would you admit his testimony into evidence from the Tadic trial into this trial? And I would suggest that you would not. And the reason we're objecting to these and what distinguishes these from other documents is that these are not contemporaneous but they are reflective recollections of what happened years before the event, and for that to be admissible, we think the witness ought to be here to be questioned about it. And that's difference between other documents and these documents like Tintor, Mrs. Plavsic book, and this, because when a witness is simply recounting his recollection after the fact of an event, that's like testimony, and that's in a different category than contemporaneous things that are said at the time, and that's why we think that you have throughout the case drawn a line for admitting contemporaneous documents that a witness could comment on and not admitting documents which were not contemporaneous but were -- where people were reflecting upon events that they'd experienced, and we believe that that affects the fairness of the trial and not necessarily a question of reliability. Testimony would be reliable, but nevertheless, we don't think it should be admissible without a witness coming and being able to ask the witness about that recollection that they're giving about past events. So that's the basis for our objection, and we think that by admitting this and having it go to the weight, it defeats the purpose of our objection, which is that the fairness of the trial is maintained by not allowing people to be giving evidence on reflection of events that occurred earlier. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, if I may. A moment's reflection -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll also try to listen to the French transcript, I take it. I was about to say that a moment's reflection, maybe not even that, would make clear that this is not analogous to testimony. If it's analogous to anything, it's far more analogous to the Assembly sessions, for example, which both parties agreed should properly be before the Court and are indeed before the Court. We are not suggesting that everything that is said at any point should be admitted to the Court. It's a case-by-case basis. What I am saying is that this bears no relationship to the rationale which would preclude the admission of previous testimony without abiding by the lex specialis provided. If you're going to draw any analogy at all, I suggest you -- that the analogies relevant here militate strongly in favour of admission, because we've admitted documents of the -- of the same sort. So when you have a document like this intended to for dissemination generally during the events in question, that is during the course of the conflict through an official publication by an official, that's without -- setting aside efforts to spill over into other potential documents, looking at this -- this particular document or any documents that are exactly of that nature, it's clear that there's more than ample reliability and they fall within the category of documents that we have admitted without question, and both sides have urged the Court to admit and consider in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think this is just a storm in a teacup. The part read to the witness is very short paragraph, and the witness confirmed to a certain extent with the content of the paragraph. So I didn't see any problem with admitting that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President. Just to clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's just so we don't get lost. I referred to what technically constitutes three paragraphs but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. But I limited to the one paragraph starting with "How did you arm the people?" I think that's the part that was read to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah but I -- no, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, I'd like -- if you need other paragraphs, why don't you put those to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I did, Mr. President. I talked about the battle at Faletici, the confrontation with Muslim forces. That's -- and I indicated to him that was contained in the next full paragraph, so I think I explicitly referred to the paragraph that begins: "How did you arm the people," and then the next small paragraph and the next full paragraph after that. Those were very explicit references - if the Court will check the transcript - with the paraphrase of what that contained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you gave the para -- the transcript page and line number?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. 41 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 41, from line 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct. So it ends "Our greatest success was taking the weapons and equipment from Faletici."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Faletici.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And as he continues in the next full paragraph, "after," et cetera. That's just what I referred to a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I referred to that first paragraph which ends with that sentence in order to orient the witness. And then I said: "As he continues in the next full paragraph after that, it talks about a confrontation at Faletici between the forces," et cetera, et cetera. All that's contained in the paragraph that begins: "It was probably Gagovic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
