utterances.text: I'm not sure the witness answered or commented anything about the next paragraph but let's leave it. I will have a consultation with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will defer the ruling on this issue in due course. Yes, let's continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Gagovic, I want to follow up on the events in those particular settlements that were the object of -- or the subject of discussion on the 11th of May with Mr. Smajic, and in that connection I'd like to turn to 65 ter 32794, and these are conversations that took place some days later on the 16th of May. There are two conversations in this exhibit. Let me turn to the first one, Colonel, and that reflects a telephone call you made to Mr. Vukota asking first is he there. He says, hey there old pal. You ask what's up. He talks about pressures from all sides, from Pofalici, Velesici, Boljakov Potok, Buca Potok. They are a group of crap, unbelievable. He says he's striking but he's got no wheat, et cetera. First of all, Colonel, can you tell us who Mr. Vukota was? If you need more time to look at the document, that's fine too. I'm not trying to rush you through.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant Vukota Vukovic had a doctorate in political sciences and was a teacher at the school in Rajlovac. Since he hailed from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, he stayed behind in Rajlovac. As far as I remember, he was the one who called me. On the first day, the Muslim forces committed a massacre in Pofalici. I think that's common knowledge. Elderly people and women were -- and children were killed. Even an elderly person bearing my family name was killed. He was informing me of the fact that this group of people, of the Muslims, were heading from Buca Potok towards Zuc and Rajlovac. This was a threat to the Serbian population that had already fled from elsewhere to Rajlovac. In that conversation I told him, well, you do have these forces, and put up resistance. Don't allow them to break through. From what I can see here, he was saying that they were putting up resistance but said that they were lacking in grain. I think he meant ammunition. That's all that I remember of this conversation with Mr. Vukota Vukotic, unless there was another person by that name, but I don't think so. He worked in the military school centre in Rajlovac. He was not within -- under the command of the corps forces. He worked there as a person who had a Ph.D.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And can you continue to read the rest of the exhibit, the rest of the document where there's another phone call between you and Vukota. Is that a continuation of the same issue regarding with a little more specificity about what should be targeted?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: That conversation happened on the same day, I'm sure. I asked about the situation in the field. I asked if they were able to resist these manic hordes, as I called them, that were advancing toward the population. The answer was that they were still advancing and that with some assistance they would be able to prevent these attacks. It was common knowledge that if the JNA provided support, then they would provide a barrage fire between the parties to the conflict. In this way they would halt these forces, would not allow them to advance. They would be forced to stay where they were or even pushed back to the positions that they started from. On that same day, I spoke to General MacKenzie and Fikret Abdic, but I don't see any record of my conversations here. General MacKenzie intervened with the president of the Presidency, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic. In the afternoon hours, the attack against Rajlovac across Zuc was aborted, was stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And with respect to barrage fire, that's the -- if we look at the first page of the first intercept --

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't get a translation, Colonel. I was just asking you that you mentioned common knowledge that JNA provided support. That's a reflection of the exchange between you and Vukota, "Just tell me where I should cover you from," and his comments, "Strike with all your strength on those. You won't be wrong;" correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: You see, the terminology used by people who were not familiar with military matters was quite random. In the army, you cannot fire with all your might. You need to use precision fire. You need to open fire only in the areas where the population is to be protected, to prevent this horde from making an onslaught and repeating the massacre that was committed in Pofalici where they killed everyone in their way. There were women and children killed, even an elderly pair aged 99 who were not even able to move or go out of their house. This is where the home of General Mladic's mother was located as well --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel --

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: -- that's to say in Pofalici. It was torched that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel --

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: He didn't know that his mother had managed to flee and he was addressing --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I -- again, you've moved beyond my questions and that's why I interrupted?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender 65 ter 32794, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P6073, thank you. P6073.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. So pending the Chamber's ruling, shall we mark it for identification, the Exhibit P6072. That's Bjelica interview. We'll mark it for identification pending the Chamber's ruling. Please continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, in your statement, in paragraph 36, you talk about co-operation with the legal representatives of the people in the corps's zone of responsibility. I'm sorry. I'm going to get to that in just a moment, but I want to ask you one follow-up question to the documents we just looked at. We looked at a conversation you had with Mr. Smajic on the 11th of May, and we then looked at another conversation on the 16th of May. I just wanted to turn quickly to your testimony in the Dragomir Milosevic case at pages 8706 and 8707, because it referred to a date in between that time. And there you say, and I'm quoting now: "I had full control over members of the 4th Corps --" And the question was, by the way, whether or not you, in terms of military control, whether you had full, complete control, and that's the question you were -- as acting corps commander, and that's the question you were asked. And then you said quote: "I had full control over members of the 4th Corps, but I did not have full control over the Territorial Defence troops. That was established on the 12th of May by Republika Srpska in an effort to start putting together its own armed forces, its own army." And I just -- I wanted you to confirm that that was your testimony in the Dragomir Milosevic case, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I did say something along those lines in my evidence and that's exactly how it happened. The Territorial Defence of the Serb republic, that's to say the municipalities inhabited by the Serbs, was at municipal level, at local commune level. The municipalities established Crisis Staffs and this part of the Territorial Defence, which was the territorial side of it, the immobile one, was under the command of the Crisis Staffs. The corps command had under its command the operative and manoeuvre units. My statement was along those lines. As a stand-in commander of the corps, I was fully apprised about -- of everything that was happening in the area that was under the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, in -- I note that I am at about the allocated time. However, I wanted to mention that in view of the circumstances, the videolink, the nature of the intercepts, the longer time taken by the accused, what I hope is my focus on relevant issues, I hope that the Court will permit me to continue, but I wanted to note my awareness of the allocation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please proceed. But do you think you can finish before the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm going to try. I think that is a genuine possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, just before we paused there, I had indicated to you that I wanted to ask you about paragraph 36 of your statement where you talk about co-operating with both Mico Stanisic, the Serbian minister of the interior, and Delimustafic, the Muslim minister. And in that connection, I wanted to turn your attention to 65 ter 32789. Now, this is a very short conversation, Colonel, that took place on the 14th of May. You get a phone call from the communications centre of the Serbian ministry indicating that the minister wants to speak to you. He says -- he identifies himself as Mico Stanisic and asks if you're okay. You say great. Asks what's up. You say, "Well, we are waging war." He says due to the confidence of the number, I am not going to -- I just wanted to tell you that I'm here in Vraca. So you can call me if you need anything." And he gives you what appear to be a couple of code-names, Karlo and Miler. As we see in other references, Miler is apparently a reference to him. This is a reflection, Colonel, of one brief contact you had with Mr. Stanic?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Then I would tender this, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a telephone contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit P6074. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I wanted to bring -- also draw your attention to your contact with at least one other Bosnian Serb political or military official, and you had repeated contact with Mr. Prstojevic; is that correct? The head of the Crisis Staff and military figure in Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, a military figure, I'm not sure about that, but he was the president of the Serb municipality of Ilidza, and by virtue of his position he was also the commander of the Crisis Staff. The municipality of Ilidza fell under the area of responsibility of the 4th Corps, and that they knew that the army was the one that that protected the civilian population. They had a small force and they had had already two attacks by the Muslim forces, and by that time they had quite a few victims --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, please?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: -- and after the 14th of May -- yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's an example of what I'm -- just describing to you. I asked you a simple question and you proceeded to use that as a platform for telling me everything you think I might want to hear about Ilidza. So please wait for the question. Okay. By the way, when you say -- when you say you're not sure about him being a military figure, does that mean you don't know -- you didn't know at the time whether he was involved in military affairs or is that a kind of subtle criticism of his military prowess?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely. He did not have military training. It's just his position made him number one at the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Let me look quickly at three phone calls you had with him. The first one is D01217. It's very short. I'm looking to see whether you have it in front of you yet. Ah. I'm not trying to rush the registrar. Okay. It's Prstojevic calling you again. You say, "Hello, Nedzo." He says "Great leader," to you, and he's indicating he doesn't have powder for recoilless guns and asks if it can be brought to him and notes that four personnel carriers are in the middle of combat. In connection with the same matter I wanted to turn to P5667 before I seek any comment from you. The previous conversation was on the 14th of May. This is on the 15th of May. The initial part of the conversation is trying to get ahold of Prstojevic. You tell him, "You wanted to speak to me Nedeljko. Good morning." He says, "Good morning. Listen, great leader," and you say there are no great leaders we are all, et cetera, and he tells you he needs urgent protection and he needs two armoured personnel carriers. And you go on to explain to him that essentially armoured personnel carriers don't grow on trees and in any event, you know the terrain he's talking about and you think infantry alone will do. And you can look at the second page of the intercept to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Ilidza was, I would say, one of rare Serb populated areas in Sarajevo attacked by Muslim armed forces on two occasions. They suffered civilian losses, and of course the JNA, because there were no particular armed forces there except for the weak Territorial Defence, and there was this prior decision by the Presidency and the command of the military district that on the line between Serb territorial forces and the Muslim forces --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, Colonel, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: -- that a mechanised unit would come --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It may be the case that the accused wants to ask you about the precise circumstances in Ilidza in respect of the TO, the JNA, and so forth, but I'm focusing for the moment on your contact with and relationship with Mr. Prstojevic, and I might as well bring your attention to one further document in connection with that. That's 65 ter 30 -- 32791?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to correct something in the record. On page 56, line 22, the witness said mechanised units that were using those APCs, and he probably meant to relate the APCs with the conversation under review, and that's not in the transcript. That mechanised unit was placed between the warring parties, and Prstojevic is obviously asking for those same APCs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gagovic, did you hear that? Do you confirm it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think I've said that. That was a JNA unit that was on the separation line between the armed forces of the Serbian Territorial Defence on one hand and Muslim armed forces on the other hand, and naturally all those municipalities and all these units wanted to have some armour, and they wanted us to assign those two APCs to them to feel safer when they toured positions in those armoured personnel carriers. And I told them that armour is not to be used in those hills. They should instead build a fortification for cover.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on. Do you have the intercept Mr. Tieger referred to in front of you? Yes. Please continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, in this intercept, Colonel, we see once again a conversation. This was on the 16th. So we've seen them three days in a row. We see Mr. Prstojevic getting in contact with you again. We see the top of page 3 in the English and it's the middle of your page 3, I believe. He reaches you. "Hello. He's here. You can talk to him, just one moment, please." You say yes. Mr. Prstojevic again says, "Great leader, I salute you." You say, "Hi there." Some pleasantries are exchanged. Then he goes on to talk about the situation and some of his needs. You can read on to see if that generally reflects the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't see where --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's -- go past the first two pages and get to the third page of your transcript, Colonel. He -- after the introductory portion I talked about, he goes on to talk about the people at Orao, his need for a trailer truck, and asking you to assist him in sorting that out. Then he also talks about the situation at Buca Potok, et cetera. Did you see that in the transcript, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see that passage, but I don't see anything particular about it apart from -- can I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, that's --

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Apart from the fact that Prstojevic was asking for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, what is your question, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do these three intercepts, Colonel, reflect the general tone of your contact with and Mr. Prstojevic and the general frequently of that contact? Or was this an unusually busy period in your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: That was a common occurrence precisely in those days because Ilidza was attacked for the second time and it was in danger. Some Muslims had already managed to get in the settlement itself, and we had an intercept, including Abdic, where we were trying to intervene to repel those Muslim forces which we actually managed to do. And he is asking here for another vehicle apart from the two APCs in order to be able to conduct some other business, and I told him that the JNA was not in a position to help him. He should go to Orlovo. They had that industry and could give him such vehicles. I don't know why he addresses me as "Great leader." He must be using that regional custom. But at one point I told him that we don't have any more great leaders, that he should stop, but I see that it's mentioned several times here. Ilidza, generally speaking, was the most exposed part of Serbian Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd tender 32791, Mr. President. I have one --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted as Exhibit D6075.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have one additional document, maybe two, but I'd suggest we take the break now otherwise everyone's going to be a little edgy. I mean, obviously I'm at the Court's disposal. I can do what you want, but my suggestion would be we simply break now and I'll conclude very quickly when we resume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How long would you need, Mr. Tieger, could conclude?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, one document and one transcript reference. I could optimistically say -- well, I mean these things are taking five to ten minutes and sometimes longer if we get a little --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could conclude in five minutes, please --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't know that I can, but I'll do my best. Can we turn please to P32787. I'm sorry. That's 65 ter 32787. My apologies. The registrar may have understood without even mentioning that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, you testified during the Dragomir Milosevic case at page 8706 that you were in constant contact with, among other people, Hasan Efendic. And this is a telephone conversation with Colonel Efendic. First of all, can you confirm that that was your testimony in the Dragomir Milosevic case, and then I'll move on to ask -- talk about the intercept.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, in this particular conversation on the 17th of May, the two of you are talking about -- reach each other and provide each other with an update on events including the discussion about movement from and within the barracks and what happens to the weaponry; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I can see, that's how the conversation went.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And then as we continue, there's a reference by Colonel Efendic to the hope that people shouldn't get killed on both sides and then the expression of the view that they're going to be killed, and you say to him, "I agree completely that the lives of people are the priority." And Efendic continues: "Let me tell you, they'll get killed." So you're discussing the risk to various -- to people within Sarajevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then you talk about who has been talking about various issues of various people, who is in charge. Efendic suggests that you're the boss, and you're the boss to Kukanjac as well. You say, "The hell I am. It's just a coincidence," et cetera. You goes on to say you've always been in favour of peaceful solutions and you feel bad that a single bullet was shot in this town in the first place. Is that a -- sorry, I didn't hear your response, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear what the Colonel said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, the interpreter did not hear what you said. If you could just --

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Is that an accurate reflection as far as you recall --

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: First of all it's a conversation that I had with Hasan Efendic, I believe at his initiative, but I'm not sure. I can barely read this. It's a manuscript. I had problems with a group of my own members of the armed forces that went renegade and started attacking barracks under blockade and then they were also firing from mortars at JNA units in Lukavica and forced the JNA members to respond with fire, and in this exchange civilian population could suffer losses too. I was saying, though, that there is nothing more valuable than human life, and that's what we should strive for, but he stressed that he was impotent ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's time to take a break. We'll break for 45 minutes and resume at 20 past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, just before the recess, you were talking a bit about the conversation you had with Hasan Efendic, and you had mentioned the fact that the JNA received fire and responded with fire and in this exchange civilian population could suffer losses too. And then you related that back to a comment in the intercept concerning the lives of people being the priority. So that's by way of background. If we look at page 2 of the -- I think it's fairly deep into the conversation, it's almost towards the end of the conversation, as mentioned before, you talk about your regret -- or you express to Efendic your regress that a single bullet was fired in the first place in the town, and then Efendic says, "Well, buddy, you're destroying it." And then by way of response, you ask -- you tell Efendic to ask a commander there whether they were allowed to fire a bullet before someone fired at them.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then -- and then you tell him with respect -- apparently with respect to his comment well, fuck it -- excuse me, well, buddy, you're destroying it. You say that that status has remained the same, not firing apparently until --

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have that document with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't realise it had been moved. Let's try to get that back in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, that is 32787, 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't find it here, the bit that he's reading. In this document, there is the conversation between me and Hasan Efendic about the evacuation of the cadets of the military school from the Marsal Tito Barracks. That was the drift of the conversation. The two of us were talking about the possible scenarios of what could happen unless a peaceful evacuation of the barracks is allowed. We concluded that this would not be to the benefit of either of the sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The part I'm referring to --

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't see where it is where the two of us --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It should begin on page 4 of the transcript in front of you, the B/C/S transcript.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Cadja was on the commission that was negotiating the blockade of the barracks on behalf of the JNA General Staff. In this section, we're not talking about any fighting, exchange of fire or anything. Hasan didn't know what my function was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And we went over that a little bit earlier. The part I'm referring your attention to, look down to about the bottom two -- the bottom third of the page, and then you say, "No. No. I've always been in favour, as they say, and the peaceful solutions." And that's where you say you feel bad that a single bullet was fired. He said --

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: He says --

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: In our conversation, he was accusing me of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gagovic, please. Could you hear the question and answer it, please. So let Mr. Tieger complete his question first.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. I realise it's difficult given the lag sometimes to know when to begin. So as you complete that portion of your discussion with Mr. Efendic you continue - and that continuation of the discussion will be found at the top of page 5 of your transcript - you say to ask him, apparently, Enver, about whether they're -- he's allowed to fire a bullet before someone fires, and then you say that status is the same, and then by way of reacting apparently to Efendic saying, "Well, buddy, you're destroying it." You point out: "But fuck it. You know when a shooting occurs, then you know how the army reacts. They fire with whatever they have. That's it." And that was all part of your discussion with Mr. Efendic to explain the concerns he had about the city being destroyed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. This is an odd conversation. I remember my conversation with Hasan Efendic well. He was offering me the duty of the commander of the Territorial Defence for Bosnia-Herzegovina. He wanted me to take up that duty because the cadets and the last of the forces of the JNA were supposed to leave the territory of the BH. I suggested that he found -- find a common language with the commander of the Territorial Defence, because they were Bosnians, whereas I was from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. I said that as soon as they allowed me to leave, as soon as the blockade of the barracks was lifted, that I would leave for my homeland. I don't know about the exchange of fire. There may have been some. But this was at the time when I was still the commander of the army. That was the 17th of May. I had already reformed the JNA. By the 20th of January, the transfer of all the members of the JNA who were from Yugoslavia was supposed to take place to Yugoslavia. The 17th, the 19th of May, up to the 1st of June, I was there with my assistant for political work, Colonel Jakovljevic, two members of the escort, and a driver. However, at that point I did not offer as an explanation the fact that I didn't have an army. Rather --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No. I think you had previously discussed the -- the issue of the JNA firing in response. It appears this is as far as we'll get with further elaboration of this conversation, so I'll move on quickly to the last very short subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I'll tender this conversation as an intercept, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. This will be admitted as Exhibit P6076.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the last thing I have, Colonel, is just to ask you to confirm something you said in the Dragomir Milosevic case when you were talking about who you were in contact with. I had mentioned earlier that you testified about being in constant contact with Colonel Hasan Efendic, and that's found at page 8706, and what you said there is, I quote, and after talking about being in constant contact -- well, I'll read the whole paragraph. "I was in constant contact with the subordinate commands. I was in constant contact with Fikret Abdic, a member of the BH Presidency; with General MacKenzie; with Colm Doyle until the 7th of May, his tour of duty ended then; and I was in constant contact with Colonel Hasan Efendic, the commander of the Main Staff of Bosnia-Herzegovina; and -- and with the leadership of Republika Srpska. "Q. By leadership of Republika Srpska, who in particular are you referring to, sir?" That's a quote of the question that was asked. And then you answered: "Well, specifically, we were in communication with the President of Republika Srpska, Radovan Karadzic, at the time." And then you go on to explain that you were in contact with your subordinate commands by telephone. Can I ask you simply to confirm that that was your testimony in the Dragomir Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: I never change my evidence. There's no reason for it. We were really in contact with all these institutions and individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I have nothing further, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, your Excellency, several questions, and I will do my best to be as short as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, sir, I need a few clarifications, brief ones.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us start from the last. Are there two Hasan Efendics, or is that the same Hasan Efendic who was elected on the 6th of April, or the 8th of April, and who replaced General Bajcetic.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: That's the same Hasan. There was one Colonel Hasan Efendic who was commander of the Main Staff of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, of the Muslim Croat part that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever see the directive that he issued on the 12th of April and re-issued on the 28th or 29th of April about placing extensive obstacles on roads and barricades and attacks on the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did have this order of his. I believe that we intervened with him as well as with the president of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Alija Izetbegovic, on this issue. Alija Izetbegovic said that it was something that the commander did independently and that this was not the position of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber what was going on in the field in view of the 22nd of April and the attack on Ilidza, as well as the 2nd and the 3rd of May in Sarajevo, and the 15th of May in Tuzla? Were these developments the result of what the Presidency intended or the result of the orders of Hasan Efendic?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: What happened in reality was the result of what Hasan Efendic wanted, all these attacks on the barracks --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Although the witness answered. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm objecting because I don't see how this arises from the cross-examination. Furthermore, it's in elaboration of the accused's examination-in-chief, insofar as I can recall, apparently referring to documents that no one bothered to upload so we never saw the translation for. So it's -- it's not comprehensible to me why we are revisiting the statement and the examination-in-chief when not triggered by inquiries made in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My learned friend Mr. Tieger has suggested in his question -- questions that the JNA had demonstrated their intention to open fire on the town while representing Hasan Efendic only as a peace-loving lamb. Instead, we can see that in this document he said that he should have opened fire sooner. I wanted to offer an opportunity to the witness to tell us who this man was and what the consequences of his actions were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you opted not to tender that document or deal with this document with that witness but now your going to deal with it. Is that the case as indicated by Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only wanted -- I don't know if the Prosecution tendered this document, 32787. I believe that the Prosecution tendered this document, and I want the witness to give us a more in depth insight into it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I understood that you were going to deal with one of -- there were three documents that were not translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, those three documents that were not translated, we've abandoned those because they were admitted under different numbers so we're finished with that. And I think that what Mr. Tieger is referring to some intercepts that we had thought we might use during the direct examination but opted not to use them, one of the reasons being that we hadn't gotten anybody to send them to Ram in Belgrade. So this I think falls squarely on the issue of whether the Prosecution's intercepts that it played with Efendic is something that Dr. Karadzic is entitled to respond to by showing the activities of Efendic at the same time period.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, whether it's dispositive on this issue or not I am not sure, but it's not accurate to say that I was referring to intercepts. I understood the accused to be turning now to 1D10067, as I think the Court did as well, and in the manner that I don't think is appropriate given the fact that he declined to do so at the appropriate time. That's what I understand this is about, that we're re-opening the direct examination for that reason. But in any event, that's what I was referring to and not intercepts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. That document is already admitted, so I don't believe that Dr. Karadzic is seeking to admit it through the back door during his re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then shall we move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. Perhaps I wasn't clear enough. I was dealing with the last document tendered by the Prosecution, 32787, the conversation between Colonel Gagovic and Colonel Efendic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, have a look at page 2, the portion where Efendic says: "The only thing we're doing is guaranteeing freedom for the families, the cadets, and everyone else." And he wants to disarm the artillery. Do you see that? It's the bottom half of page 2.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: I understand this without looking at the document. I recall this conversation with him. He could not be trusted precisely for the reason that he decided that as many members of the JNA as possible be captured, neutralised, killed, and at any rate not allowed to cross the border into the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. This decision of his was already being implemented on the 2nd of May and the 3rd of May, and on the 15th -- this was in Sarajevo, and on the 15th of May in Tuzla. There was a unit deployed in Husinjski Rudara [phoen] barracks, and there over a hundred members of the JNA came in harm's way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So on the 17th of May you weren't able to trust his guarantees; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, definitely. There was a group of people who was speaking to the General Staff and with some other institutions of Bosnia-Herzegovina, including Fikret Abdic and Hasan Efendic about the lifting of the blockade of the barracks. And in this particular instance I said that this man could not be trusted in view of what his previous actions were. So he seized an opportunity in the case of these attacks to say, "Well, you opened fire previously," and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I'm waiting for interpretation, and please do so as well. Let me ask you this: It has to do with those telephone conversations. Can you tell us where Varos was? Where were you, where was Jankovic, and where was Mladic, physically?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Physically, Mladic was in Han Pijesak. Varos was in the Marsal Tito barracks under a blockade. I was in the Lukavica barracks. And Jankovic was the person who arrived there with a team of people to evacuate the cadets of the secondary military school and the military academy from the Marsal Tito Barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What is the distance between you and the Marsal Tito Barracks and between you and Mladic in Han Pijesak approximately?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Approximately between me and Mladic there was about 70 kilometres. I'm not sure. And between me and Marsal Tito Barracks there was about 6 to 7 kilometres approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel, sir. I just wanted to establish whether any of your collocutors were in the same room with somebody else, but they were not, were they?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. We were all in different locations as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether you were abreast of the law of All People's Defence and the doctrine of armed people?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I knew those things well. I had been through all the military schools. I was also familiar with international laws and the provisions of the Geneva Conventions dealing with prisoners of war and the civilian population and so on and so forth. So I was familiar with all those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us who was it who had the right to use Territorial Defence units? Which legal entities had the right to use Territorial Defence units?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, there --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- it's a fact that territorial units were connected to their own territories, as the name has it. They are connected to municipalities, local communes, or companies. Even universities in Sarajevo had their own Territorial Defence units. And municipalities had the right to use them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The last part of your question was very much leading. Bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I apologise. I'm in a hurry, that's why. But I'm convinced that the colonel is very familiar with that law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this, Colonel, sir, because you were asked about your influence, i.e., your connections with the territorial units and the units of the Territorial Defence that were under the authority of the municipality. As far as you know, when it comes to the Territorial Defence organisation, was anything done against the law at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: No, nothing. This would be my shortest answer: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were also asked, i.e., you were requested to confirm that you had contacts with the President of Republika Srpska -- or, rather, the president of the Presidency at the time, Mr. Karadzic. Can you tell the Trial Chamber whether Karadzic ever asked you to do something that would be contrary to the law or that would be against your role as the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Just the opposite. For as long as I was in that position and while General Djurdjevac was in that position before me, you never tried to request us to do anything against the law. I personally can say that you requested your subordinates, your officers, not to dirty their hands and treat the civilians, prisoners of war, and especially the wounded in an inhuman way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While you were there did the JNA intentionally open fire on civilians in Sarajevo? Did they do anything else in order to terrorise the civilians in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Never. No single shell was ever fired to inflict losses on civilians. However, when fire was opened on the barracks, when mortar fire and higher calibre fire was opened by the Muslim formations, things like that happened. I believe that General Lewis MacKenzie understood that. He was the UNPROFOR commander. However, those armed Muslim components had mobile units on vehicles on which they mounted mortars, and they would leap from one place to another. They opened fire. So sometimes the civilian population suffered because fire was opened on them. On one such occasion two soldiers were killed at the Lukavica barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know somebody on the Serbian side starting from the highest republican level to the municipal level who advocated a position that the civilian population in Sarajevo had to be fired upon and terrorised? Did you ever come across such an institution or such an individual?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: I never came across such an individual or such an institution. At the time when I was there, the Serbian people did not have any aspirations towards Sarajevo. They didn't have any aspirations whatsoever towards Sarajevo. They only organised the defence of their lives, their houses, their properties that surrounded Sarajevo. However, you have to understand that Sarajevo was under blockade from inside, not from the outside. Those people who wanted to leave Sarajevo could not leave it because of the internal blockade that was organised by -- organised by the Muslims. Only those with fat pockets could bribe somebody and leave the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel, sir. Just one more document and one more question. A reference was made here, Colonel Miletic, maybe he was major, I don't know what his rank was, he was in a conversation with you. Where was he at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D6303.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Miletic was in Rajlovac. He worked in a factory that produced ... There was some interruptions. I don't know whether I completed my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, only half of your answer was recorded. You said that he was in Rajlovac. Was there a military institution there? Were there barracks there?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: The centre of military schools was there, the airforce academy, and the secondary military school was there. There was an auxiliary airport there that was used for the training of some of those students and high school students.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please take a look at the document in front of you. This is an intercepted conversation between you and Miletic. Could you please tell us whether this document shows clearly who was shooting at whom. Zekerijah says one thing and Miletic tells you what he told you. Can you tell us what transpired on the 11th of May?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Fikret Abdic got involved in that conversation. He was in charge of contacts with the JNA, General MacKenzie, and all the others who were there. However, none of them, including me personally, could conclude where the fire came from and disturbed people in the suburbs of Sarajevo and Rajlovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Miletic offered you his telephone to demonstrate to you the thunder going on in his territory and the shooting that comes from the surrounding areas. Did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I could hear the noise, but even the scouts noticed that in that area of Rajlica [as interpreted] one could observe mortar shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Whose shells were those? Who fired them?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Members of Muslim formations did that. I believe that Sefer Halilovic was in command of those forces. Later on, he became the commander of the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel, sir. I have no further questions. Thank you very much for your effort in coming to the location to provide your evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you tendering that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, your Excellency. I would like to tender 6303.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be the next Defence exhibit. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, in light of the nature of the questioning that is about the sounds, and I think the Court will need it well to have the audio to hear whether, in fact, the alleged sounds can be heard. So we -- we will provide that audio. I think the nature of the questioning pretty much compels that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So shall we give that same number? Yes, we'll admit it together with the audio. I will consult the registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We will admit it together with the audio.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And the document assigned shall be D2740 together with the audio. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Gagovic, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Chamber, I'd like to thank you for your co-operation. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, I take it the next witness is ready, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah, it -- as long as we're at a juncture without a witness in the courtroom, I was wondering if the Court would allow me an me an opportunity to clarify something that Mr. Robinson raised earlier about a filing by the Prosecution. And I discussed this with him. I think he would like the Prosecution to clarify this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's about that intercept?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's about the filing to the -- in response to the accused's motion for reconsideration regarding Defence intercepts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson made the representation earlier that the Prosecution's position was that in the absence of the type of authentication protocol that had -- that the Prosecution had gone through during the course of its case with respect to intercepts, that we would object to the authenticity of intercepts. That's not what the motion was intended to convey. I've read it again and think we didn't convey that, but I understand that some confusion exists. We cited, for example, to the best of my recollection, an oral representation or a response made in court, during which the Prosecution said basically now that the Defence has required the Prosecution to go through this entire elaborate process, it wants to be free of the same requirement. We noted that in passing but then made clear, nevertheless, we maintain our original position that the body of intercepts from the general sources presented are reliable and authentic and didn't object to that. So when there's a reference in the motion to the sources of the intercepts, that -- that's intended to convey the broad source, not -- not the -- not the specific limited materials that were the object of scrutiny during the course of the Prosecution case. So we -- in the motion, we noted that we didn't think the Defence had originally given the Court any information about the source of those intercepts, and that might be one of the reasons why the Court denied the motion, and we mentioned that in the response to the motion for reconsideration, but I didn't want us to be understood as insisting, as Mr. Robinson suggested earlier, that they needed to go through the elaborate exercise of recalling individual intercept operators. We were trying to convey that we considered the broad categories, and I think the Court knows those three broad categories of intercepts, to be authenticated and reliable. So I didn't want the Defence to be unfairly disadvantaged by a misinterpretation of what we had submitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you like to add anything, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. I appreciate Mr. Tieger stating that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There are a couple of things that I'd like to raise with you, Mr. Robinson, before we hear the next witness's evidence. First, we are seized of a correspondence from the Embassy of Bosnia-Herzegovina which was filed on the 11th of January this year, indicating that Mr. Edin Garaplija, in relation to whom the Chamber issued a subpoena to testify, was banned from entering any Schengen state. Do you have any submission to make in relation to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. With respect to -- as soon as we received that, I contacted the VWS and asked them to determine whether or not that ban would prohibit him from coming as part of the subpoena, and if it does, indicated that we would be prepared to make a motion for a safe conduct order so that he could come notwithstanding that ban, but I haven't gotten any response yet from them. So as soon as I do, I will let the Chamber know and take that step if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. And the next one is related to the signed statement of Trifko Pljevaljcic, the last witness scheduled for this week. The Chamber would like to hear from you as to the relevance of this -- of this statement to the Defence case, in particular paragraphs 2 to 15, which cover the period 1989 to 1990. Not necessarily now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Actually, Mr. President, perhaps Dr. Karadzic, if he wants to address this now we could do it, because we have been discussing that actually with the Prosecution and with Dr. Karadzic concerning the relevance of the events in Foca, and I think Dr. Karadzic is prepared to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is he ready to answer that question? He can answer the question later or today or tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Perhaps it would be better if we did it in the morning then, first thing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we bring in the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Would the witness take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hatchett. Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Professor Hatchett.

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to call up 1D05638 in e-court, please. Professor Hatchett, or Dr. Hatchett, I don't know how to refer to you, your career is rather impressive. Have you provided a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT
utterances.text: I have, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you see that statement in front of you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you sign the statement?

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT
utterances.text: Yes, I did. That's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this statement truly reflect what you stated for the benefit of the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were -- I were to put the same questions to you today in this courtroom, would your answers be more or less the same as they are in the statements of yours?

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT
utterances.text: Yes, my answer would be the same as I've indicated here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this statement pursuant to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. With respect to the associated exhibits, there's three that we're tendering. One is the excerpt of the video, which is 1D5593, and then the map and the article in the newspaper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you are not tendering the entire video?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objections, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So witness's 92 ter statement as well as three associated exhibits will be admitted into evidence. Let us give the numbers for them now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: They shall be given numbers D2741 to D2744. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And now I'm going to read a short summary of Dr. Ronald Hatchett's statement in English. [In English] Dr. Ronald Hatchett served for 20 years as a United States airforce officer working on intelligence and politico-military affairs. After his military service, he served as a civilian representative of the United States Secretary of Defence for multinational security organisations in Europe. After leaving government service in 1988, Dr. Hatchett taught at universities in Texas and recently retired as the director of the centre for global studies at Schreiner University. On 13 to 18th September, 1992, Dr. Hatchett visited Pale with other members of the Lord Byron Foundation for Balkan Studies, a non-Partisan research centre devoted to the -- to studying affairs in the Balkans. During his time in Pale, Dr. Hatchett participated in meetings with President Karadzic and other Bosnian Serb civilian and military leaders. He was struck by the efforts President Karadzic was willing to make to end the fighting and save civilian lives. In particular, when in the midst of the discussion General Tolimir tried to get Dr. Hatchett to say as a former military officer that the way to end the fighting around Sarajevo was an all out Serbian military assault, Dr. Karadzic firmly rebuked him saying, "I'm not going to launch a major military assault on a city full of people, killing thousands on both sides, when I know that we will not be allowed to keep this territory in a peace agreement." During the discussions, at no time did Dr. Hatchett ever hear Radovan Karadzic express the view that the Republika Srpska should be ethnically pure and not include Bosnian Muslims and Croats. Hatchett videotaped an interview with Dr. Karadzic during his visit to Pale. He asked Dr. Karadzic what his position was on ethnic cleansing. Dr. Karadzic responded that ethnic cleansing has never been the policy of Republika Srpska and that after the end of the war, it ought to be the obligation of all three republics to enable the refugees to -- who wish to come back to their own homes to do so. Dr. Hatchett had a private meeting with President Karadzic during his trip to Pale. Dr. Karadzic told him that he had a proposal for ending the war and asked Dr. Hatchett to take it back to the highest level of the -- that he could reach in the United States government. Dr. Karadzic's proposal was that Bosnia will remain a single country comprised of two autonomous republics, Republika Srpska and the Muslim-Croat federation. Each republic would have their own constitution and government and will control domestic affairs within its territory, including border access. The central government will represent Bosnia in international organisations. Positions in central government will be equitably shared between Republika Srpska and Muslim-Croat federation. Bosnian territory will be split up proportion 49/51. He proposed a US meditation -- mediation at a location away from media necessary, similar to Camp David mediation between Egypt and Israel in 1979. Dr. Karadzic also provided Dr. Hatchett a map which showed the proposed division of territory. There was never any question that Muslims and Croats would be allowed to live in the Serb areas, and Serbs would be allowed to live in Muslim and Croat areas of the proposed territories and that the rights of minorities would be respected. Dr. Hatchett believes that President Karadzic genuinely wanted an end of the war and thought that as a former US government official, he might have the contacts to help him achieve this. Dr. Hatchett managed to get the proposal to President Clinton who was reportedly excited about it. However, he later learned that the proposal had been shot down by the state government -- State Department. Subsequently, the United States decided to convene negotiations in a controlled area at a military base in Dayton, Ohio. This was similar to what Dr. Karadzic had proposed in September 1994. The agreement that was reached at Dayton in November 1995 resulted in the same proportion, 41 -- 49/51 division of the territory that Dr. Karadzic had proposed in September 1994. The map produced in Dayton does not differ significantly from the map given to the -- to Dr. Hatchett by Dr. Karadzic in September 1994. The political division -- divisions agreed to in Dayton are also similar to those proposed by Dr. Karadzic in September 1994. [Interpretation] That would be a short summary of Dr. Hatchett's statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Hatchett, I'd like to ask you as a man with rich experience in military matters, have you had the opportunity to look at the nature of the war primarily around Sarajevo, and the nature of the whole conflict related to what is sometimes called a siege, that conflict in the city that lasted 42 months?

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT
utterances.text: While I was there, I was given the opportunity to visit Sarajevo. In fact, I went down into the built-up area of Sarajevo where there was still quite a significant Serbian population occupying a portion of the city living there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you continue, Mr. Hatchett, yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I was trying to define exactly where this was going, but if it's seeking some form of expert opinion, it's way too late for that. And furthermore, it -- this appears to be moving into an area that has nothing to do with the statement and was in no way notified to the Prosecution. So I'm a little -- I thought it might relate in some way, but I am having trouble seeing how it's about to, and I wanted to stop it before it moved any further if that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. President, the question I believe it was intended to elicit Dr. Hatchett's observations when he was in Sarajevo which are depicted on the video that was disclosed to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let us continue then. Would you like to respond, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I do. If there was an intention of eliciting from this witness some view of -- some opinion on documents submitted, that should have been done previously and it was not. And this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, view of -- view on documents? I don't follow. What documents do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When -- in the normal course of business if a witness is going to be asked to comment upon and evidence is going to be elicited from a witness on materials, then the -- the adverse party is notified of that, and there's been no such notification whatsoever. This is coming entirely out of the blue. It's not in the statement. It's not in the summary. It was in no way -- it's not in a proofing note. It was not -- no indication that the witness would be asked to address such issues has been provided to the Prosecution whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But speaking for myself, as long as the question is limited to his observation during his visit to Sarajevo, I don't see much problem, but I'll consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Can I also point out to you that in the summary it says during their stay in Pale his group toured the VRS positions in the hills above Sarajevo as well as the area of Gorazde. So between the disclosure of the video and this portion of the summary, I don't think there's anything wrong with asking him about his view of what he saw in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's entirely the point, Mr. President. I mean, he focused on a very narrow part. I have no issue if he wants to elaborate some ambiguity in the part that was notified, but this is frankly a kind of trick to identify a very narrow portion and then claim that it gives rise to the opportunity to raise issues that extend far broader than -- than that which was notified. Now, again, if it's about that particular portion and that particular portion only, of course it's fair, but that's not what seems to be happening. Instead, because the word "Sarajevo" is mentioned somewhere in the statement, now the Defence apparently feels free to ask them anything they want about Sarajevo. And the issue is not whether the witness is properly in a position to comment upon observations he may or may not have made, the issue is fair notice, and opportunity to prepare for cross-examination. And that's a point that Mr. Robinson raised repeatedly. We always tried to provide that, including sometimes sending proofing notes very, very late in the evening just to ensure that some notice was provided in an appropriate fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In terms of that notice, Mr. Tieger, in case of a partial Rule 92 ter witness as was indicated with respect to this witness, to what extent does one party have to notify the other as to the part that is to be led live?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's the same situation as with a viva voce witness where you provide an adequate 65 ter summary talking about -- providing a factual summary of the issues that the witness will be discussing, the evidence that will be elicited from the witness. If it's not provided, then the other side has a fair point that they're not in a position to prepare for the evidence that is sought to be elicited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, could you tell us the part of the summary that you referred to? Where is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. It's the second to last sentence: "During their stay in Pale, his group toured the VRS positions in the hills above Sarajevo, as well as the area of Gorazde."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: During ... so you referred to para-14 of his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. It's also included in paragraph 14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, instead of posing a very general question, could you put your question more specifically with respect to any part of his statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, your Excellency. Thank you. I just want to say that I believe Dr. Hatchett accepted to take my message to President Clinton and his government only because he was satisfied that my intentions were honest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's not an appropriate comment. Just put your question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Hatchett, you referred to one of the conversations where you were present wherein military logic told General Tolimir that the war has to end in victory, and you knew that I said that that would not happen. Can you tell us your conclusions about the nature of that war in Sarajevo and around Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I don't follow your question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, your Excellencies, I believe Mr. Hatchett referred to my words, "I'm not going to launch a major military assault on a city full of people," and Dr. Hatchett knew exactly what my intentions, and he had observed the city and the fighting, and I'm asking him as such what he concluded, not as an expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You could ask him how did he understood your comment or whether he understood your intention, but asking him the nature of the war with respect to that comment is far-fetched, I take it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please answer, Dr. Hatchett, the question kindly phrased by the Presiding Judge and tell us what you saw. What did you witness while you were there?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Wait, wait. I don't understand why we're going in circles like this, and I think it's -- it's particularly inappropriate to suggest that the accused has adopted the formulation of the trial Bench and then revert back to his original formulation. That's not at all what the Court was suggesting, and again it's -- these are repeated efforts to do what the -- to try to elicit evidence in a manner the Trial Chamber has said first is not appropriate and then has provided specific guidance for a potentially appropriate way to do so, which is being ignored by the accused.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I'll have to rephrase it once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Hatchett, could you tell the Chamber what you saw in Sarajevo, and how does that compare with other cities under siege?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Notice, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, it's the same issue. And I don't -- I guess this is now sort of a stand-off on who's more stubborn, Dr. Karadzic in continuing to pose the same question over and over, or me in repeatedly getting up to make the same objection which the Court has sustained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, could you advise Mr. Karadzic how to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll try again, because I wonder why Mr. Tieger is afraid of what Dr. Hatchett might answer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's not an appropriate comment at all. Unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tieger said I was stubborn, so I had to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Hatchett, can you tell us what you saw in Sarajevo, and how does that relate to the claims that the city was under siege?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what Mr. Robinson explained, but it's difficult to see the difference between this question and the previous formulations. It's the same problem. We were not advised that this witness would be offering a comparative review of cities under siege based on what he saw previously. That's not in the statement. Based on what he saw in Sarajevo. That's not in the statement. And based on a kind of quasi-expert opinion that was not noticed and that is certainly, in any event, belated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, this question doesn't relate to other cities or asking him to be an expert. He went and saw Sarajevo, and he's being asked whether or not from what he saw did the city appear to be under siege.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If it relates to issue of siege or encirclement or whatever, I would like the accused to move on. Move on to another topic, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I think we are missing a good opportunity to hear from a professional, experienced witness, and to help us understand things, but I don't have anything more. I hope that perhaps the Trial Chamber might put these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Hatchett, as you have noted, your evidence in chief was in most part -- in whole admitted in writing, and you will be further asked by the representative of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And good afternoon, Mr. Hatchett. We will be commencing, but there's only a very short time between now and when we have to adjourn, so we won't be going into too many issues before we have to adjourn. In paragraph 7 of your statement, you mention --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. You have your statement in hard copy with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to have one, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That will be forthcoming.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I had just been about to refer to paragraph 7 of your statement where you first mention your trip in September 1994 with -- to Pale with other members of the Lord Byron Foundation for Balkan Studies, which is characterised as a non-Partisan research centre devoted to studying the Balkan Peninsula in all its aspects.

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I wanted to begin by asking you about the Lord Byron centre, asking you a few more questions about it. First of all, it's correct that the reason it's named the Lord Byron Foundation, named after Lord Byron, is because as indicated on the foundation web site, because he gave his life in the fight to free Balkan Christians from Islamic rule. That's -- is it correct that that's the nature of the origin of the name of the organisation?

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT
utterances.text: I think that is correct, sir. That was a name that was selected by the primary founder of the organisation which was Dr. Srdja Trifkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in addition to Dr. Trifkovic, was Sir Alfred Sherman one of the primary founding members of the organisation?

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And is it correct that the organisation was founded, as Sir Alfred Sherman has stated, to correct what was considered a systematic propagandistic view of the Balkans? In other words, the organisation was founded to fight the -- a prevailing view of the Balkans?

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT
utterances.text: Yes. And my understanding was the organisation's purpose was to provide a more complete picture of what was underlying all of the problems of the Balkans at this time. The feeling amongst several of us was that the information that was in the media was in many ways not reflective of the actual history of the area and the events leading up to the conflict that was occurring at that time and had a decidedly anti-Serb bias in the media which we thought needed to be balanced.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In fact, the anti-Serb bias that you refer to was considered to be by the founding members quite strong. So Sir Alfred Sherman, for example, referred that the Serbs were being subjected to a pogrom from the West and that the West was beset by chronic Serbophobia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what -- if Sir Alfred really believed in this, but I can just tell you that I didn't feel that strongly about it. I did feel that the media was missing a lot in the discussion about the -- again the point of view of the Serbs in the struggle and the rights and the history of the Serbs in the area, and I joined with these others because I thought we could do some service to a better understanding of what was actually transpiring there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Staying with Sir Alfred Sherman for a moment, who has written extensively about it, as has Dr. Trifkovic, he also wrote that a -- he considered an independent Bosnia as the cornerstone of a European Islamistan. Was that consistent with the view of the foundation?

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT
utterances.text: Well, it's not consistent with my views. All I can tell you is that Sir Alfred Sherman, and perhaps Dr. Srdja Trifkovic, they have their own views about this, but I didn't share 100 per cent their views on what was happening there or the ramifications of what was happening there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you aware that Sir Alfred received the order of Njegos by Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT
utterances.text: I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you have any idea what services he provided to Republika Srpska --

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT
utterances.text: I do not know how long.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Sir Alfred along with Srdja Trifkovic wrote about and apparently believed in what they called the threat of a green corridor linking Bosnia to the east. Were you aware of their views on this particular issue?

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT
utterances.text: I was aware of those views, but as I said again, those are not my views. I didn't share that. I saw the situation in Bosnia as simply a problem of multiculturalism of three different cultural groups that were trying to find a way to live in new circumstances with the collapse of Yugoslavia. I didn't see a great conspiracy behind what was going on in this region. Maybe to the extent that perhaps Alfred Sherman did or Srdja Trifkovic did. I don't share, as I said, their points of view necessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And keep that in mind so let me just ask you about one further view that seems to be held not only by a number of representatives of the -- or officials the Lord Byron Foundation and that is contained at various places on the web site of the foundation, and that is the view that the part of the Serbophobia of the West is that -- is the establishment of this Tribunal, which is considered "a propaganda machine" which has "acted more in keeping with the processes followed by the Stalinist show trials of the late 1930s." Now, that's on the web site and that was written specifically by Mr. Bissett who was a chairman of the Lord Byron Foundation. Is that a view held by the foundation and by the members of the foundation?

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT
utterances.text: It may be a view held by Mr. Bissett and it may be a view held by others, but it's not a view that's held by me. In fact, I lent my name to this when it was first beginning, but I haven't been very active in it for the last 8 or 10 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And we are just about to adjourn, so let me just finish up that topic. Were you aware that Mr. Trifkovic, too, has written about the same issue along the same lines; that is, he's written that the Tribunal accepts the role of a political tool of its political bosses and paymasters and "its decisions are as predictable as those in Moscow in 1936"?

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT
utterances.text: I'm aware that he's written things like this, but, you know, once again I would just point out to you, Mr. Prosecutor, his views and my views are not necessarily the same. In fact, not only not necessarily, they are not the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. But just to clarify in connection with the organisation, Mr. Trifkovic is or was the executive director of the Lord --

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT
utterances.text: Yes, he is the driving force within the organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think it's the appropriate time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will adjourn for today and continue tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I advise you not to discuss with anybody else about your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 16th day of January, 2013, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.47 p.m.,
